opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't call it a fatal flaw, but there are a few things that keep bothering me.

The first is what the objective actually rewards. Next-token prediction asks the model to imitate the data distribution as faithfully as possible. That's very powerful, and it's why scaling has worked so well. But imitation and intelligence aren't the same thing. If you train on human text, you're mostly learning to reproduce the *outputs* of human thinking, not the process that produced them. A lot of the real reasoning, the false starts, the checking, the "wait, that's wrong," never gets written down. The model sees the polished answer and has to guess the hidden computation behind it. Sometimes it guesses well, and sometimes it just learns to sound like it reasoned.

The second is the structure of generation itself. Every token is one fixed-size step of computation, and once you emit it, you're committed. For easy problems that's fine. For hard problems, the amount of thinking needed is very uneven. Some steps are trivial, and some need a huge amount of search. A pure left-to-right, one-token-at-a-time model has no natural way to say "let me spend a hundred times more compute right here," or to go back and revise. Errors accumulate, and the model is trained to continue plausibly, not to stop and doubt itself.

Chain-of-thought and reinforcement learning on reasoning partly patch this. You let the model externalize its thinking into tokens, and then RL rewards outcomes rather than imitation. That's a big step, and I think it's the most important shift of the last couple of years. But it's still a patch on the same backbone. You're forcing all thinking to happen in the language channel, serialized, at token granularity. I'm not sure that's how efficient thinking should look.

The third reason comes from my background in vision. With images and video, next-token prediction feels much less natural. If you tokenize an image and predict it patch by patch, it works to some extent, but generation and understanding don't reinforce each other the way they do in language. In text, being able to predict the next word really does force you to understand. In pixels, you can spend enormous capacity predicting texture details that have nothing to do with understanding the scene. So the bet that "prediction equals understanding" seems specific to language, which is already a highly compressed, abstract signal made by humans. Once you leave that domain, the assumption starts to crack.

So my suspicion isn't that next-token prediction is wrong. It's that it has worked so well in language that people treat it as a universal principle. I think it's more of a very successful special case. The next real breakthroughs probably need some way for models to decide how much to think, to search and revise internally, and to learn from consequences rather than just imitation. Whether that grows out of the current paradigm or replaces it, I honestly don't know yet. But I'd be surprised if the final answer is just "predict the next token, but bigger."

r002.rationale: It raises concerns about next-token prediction, but does not connect skipped steps in mathematical solutions to an inherent flaw.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, my suspicion really comes from working on the training side, not from theory first. When you train a model purely on next-token prediction, you're asking it to maximize the likelihood of the next token given everything before it. That sounds fine. But think about what that objective actually rewards. It rewards fitting the surface distribution of text. It doesn't care whether the model understood why that token comes next, only that it predicts it.

The thing that bothered me is this: human text is the output of a reasoning process, but the reasoning itself is mostly missing from the data. When a mathematician writes a proof, you see the final clean steps. You don't see the twenty failed attempts, the moment they realized an approach was wrong, the backtracking. Next-token prediction learns the answer without the search that produced it. So the model becomes very good at imitating the form of thinking, and much weaker at actually doing the thing that generates that form.

And you can see this empirically. We trained models with more and more data, and the gains on knowledge and language fluency kept coming, but the gains on genuine reasoning, on problems that require trying, failing, and correcting, were much flatter. The scaling curve for memorization and the scaling curve for reasoning are not the same curve. That gap told me the objective itself is leaving something out.

There's a second issue, which is more mechanical. Next-token prediction is one-directional and teacher-forced. During training the model never sees its own mistakes. It always gets the correct prefix. So it never learns what to do when it has already gone wrong, which in real generation happens constantly. Errors compound and the model has no mechanism to recover, because it was never trained to recover.

So when I say inherent flaw, I don't mean next-token prediction is useless. It's clearly the best way we have to pour knowledge into a model. I mean it is incomplete as an objective for intelligence. It gives you a very strong prior, but something else, reinforcement learning or some form of search, has to teach the model to actually reason, to explore, to reflect on its own output. That's why I think the next stage isn't just more pretraining. It's changing what we're optimizing for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses omitted reasoning and failed attempts in human proofs, but does not state that larger models tend to skip steps in math problems.

r002.rationale: It argues that next-token prediction misses the search and reasoning behind answers, but does not connect models skipping steps in mathematical solutions to an inherent flaw.

astra-6.text:
What makes me suspicious is the gap between predicting the next token and deciding what to say. A good next token doesn’t necessarily move you toward a good overall answer. Sometimes you need to work backward from a goal, explore several possibilities, or revise an earlier assumption.

Next-token prediction can learn patterns that resemble those processes, so I wouldn’t say that proves an inherent flaw. The question is whether the training objective reliably rewards them. If a model can reduce its prediction error by reproducing familiar surface patterns, it may do that without learning the underlying structure. That’s the limitation I’d want to investigate: when does successful prediction actually require understanding, and when can you get away without it?

sol-6.1.text:
What makes me suspicious is the gap between predicting what someone would say and figuring out what is actually true. Next-token prediction rewards a model for continuing the text, but a plausible continuation can still contain a mistake.

Think about a problem where an early decision determines whether the whole solution works. The model has to generate that decision before it has written out the consequences. It can learn to anticipate those consequences, but the training objective doesn’t directly require it to check them.

I wouldn’t call that proof of an inherent flaw. Next-token prediction might be powerful enough to learn planning and verification. The question is whether it reliably encourages those abilities, or whether it often rewards shortcuts that look convincing until you test them.
